newsitem.title: USA: LME backwardation sign of free mkt - ASARCO.
newsitem.headline: LME backwardation sign of free mkt - ASARCO.

text.p: The yawning backwardation in the London Metal Exchange's flagship copper contract was just a sign of the market working normally at a time of very low red metal stockpiles, Richard de J Osborne, chairman, president and chief executive of ASARCO Inc said.

"It's the free market and clearly it's working now - it's working how it's supposed to work," Osborne said in reply to questions following a lunchtime presentation at the American Metal Market's copper seminar.
Osborne, also non-executive chairman of ASARCO's majority owned Southern Peru Copper SOUt.LM, will be honored later this evening as the annual copper Man of the Year at New York's Copper Club dinner.
The LME backwardation, or cash premium over three months contract, soared to over $300 in recent weeks, but has gradually eased back to $147/$151 by Tuesday, down from over $200 last week.
Earlier Tuesday at the same seminar, NYMEX's first vice president Neal Wolkoff said the backwardation was "anomalistic".
But Osborne said the market was very short of physical supplies of metal, and the mechanism it used to attract material into warehouses was the backwardation. "It's not a surprise to me," he added.
The sharp backwardation stretched and even broke the normal rules of copper trading as some delivered metal to the nearest exchange warehouse to exploit the cash premium, Osborne said.

When the backwardation collapses, the metal which entered warehouses usually finds its way back to consumers, he added. Nevertheless Osborne agreed that another Sumitomo-type scandal in the copper market could occur, and greater transparency was the key to avoiding this.

"The lack of clarity and lack of understanding in May, June and July last year about Sumitomo's positions gave rise to the ability of speculators, long or short, to trade based on unfounded rumors or speculation, some of which they may have had a part in putting in the market," Osborne said.
In his presentation Osborne suggested that participants could voluntarily offer details about any major position they have in the market to dampen speculation and volatility which rumors caused.
But later when questioned by reporters, Osborne added that "nobody would do it unless there was a requirement", but he was unsure of what legal format such a rule would take on LME.

Apart from putting forward this suggestion to the U.K. watchdog Securities and Investment Board's review of the LME, Osborne said he had not talked about such a proposal with the LME or any other regulator.
